subject: science
title: Data Representation: Soil pH and Seed Germination
text:
Seeds require a particular soil chemistry in order to sprout. Researchers tested how soil pH affects germination in two crop species: Species A, a common bean, and Species B, a clover. For each trial, 100 seeds were planted in identical trays of sterilized soil that had been adjusted to a fixed pH with buffered solutions. All trays were kept at 20°C and watered daily. The percent of seeds that germinated within 14 days was recorded (Table 1).

Table 1
Soil pH | Species A germination (%) | Species B germination (%)
4.5 | 8 | 3
5.0 | 22 | 11
5.5 | 41 | 26
6.0 | 58 | 49
6.5 | 66 | 72
7.0 | 71 | 80
7.5 | 63 | 74
8.0 | 44 | 55

In a second trial, trays were held at pH 6.0 and placed in growth chambers set to four soil temperatures. The number of days until the first seedling emerged in each tray was recorded (Table 2).

Table 2
Soil temperature (°C) | Species A (days) | Species B (days)
10 | 14 | 17
15 | 9 | 11
20 | 6 | 7
25 | 5 | 6

Finally, Species A seedlings that had already germinated were grown for 21 additional days at 20°C in soil of four pH values. Mean shoot height and mean root mass per seedling were then measured (Table 3).

Table 3
Soil pH | Mean shoot height (cm) | Mean root mass (g)
5.0 | 4.1 | 0.18
6.0 | 9.6 | 0.44
7.0 | 13.2 | 0.61
8.0 | 7.8 | 0.35

Soil pH influences germination in part by controlling how readily nutrients dissolve. In acidic soil, aluminum and manganese ions become more soluble and can injure the delicate tips of emerging roots. In alkaline soil, iron, zinc, and phosphorus form compounds that plant roots absorb poorly. Neither species germinated well below pH 5.0, and both showed reduced performance above pH 7.5. Growers often adjust soil chemistry before planting, adding ground limestone to raise pH or elemental sulfur to lower it.

subject: science
title: Data Representation: Wind Turbine Power Output
text:
A wind turbine converts the kinetic energy of moving air into electricity. Engineers tested two designs on the same tower site: Turbine X, which has three blades and a 20 m rotor, and Turbine Y, which has two blades and a 22 m rotor. Each turbine was exposed to steady wind at a series of speeds, and the electrical power delivered to the grid was measured (Table 1). Both turbines were programmed to shut down above 25 m/s to prevent damage.

Table 1
Wind speed (m/s) | Turbine X power (kW) | Turbine Y power (kW)
3 | 0 | 0
5 | 45 | 30
7 | 130 | 95
9 | 285 | 210
11 | 480 | 390
13 | 600 | 560
15 | 600 | 620
17 | 600 | 620
19 | 600 | 620

Table 2 lists the mean wind speed measured at the site during four months, together with the capacity factor of Turbine X. Capacity factor is the energy actually generated in a month divided by the energy the turbine would generate if it ran at its rated power for the entire month.

Table 2
Month | Mean wind speed (m/s) | Turbine X capacity factor (%)
January | 9.4 | 41
April | 8.1 | 33
July | 5.6 | 18
October | 7.9 | 31

Table 3 shows the power available in the wind passing through each rotor at three speeds, along with the percent of that power each turbine actually captured.

Table 3
Wind speed (m/s) | Available wind power (kW) | X captured (%) | Y captured (%)
7 | 320 | 41 | 30
11 | 1240 | 39 | 31
15 | 3140 | 19 | 20

The power carried by wind rises with the cube of wind speed, which is why the available power in Table 3 grows so steeply. No rotor can capture all of it; theory sets the maximum at about 59%, because air must retain enough energy to keep moving out of the way of the blades. Below a cut-in speed near 4 m/s neither turbine produced usable power, since the torque on the blades was too small to overcome friction in the drive train. Above its rated speed each turbine pitched its blades to spill excess wind, holding output constant to protect the generator.

subject: science
title: Data Representation: Tides at Coastal Stations
text:
Tides are the regular rise and fall of sea level produced mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon and, to a lesser degree, the Sun. At Harbor A an automated gauge recorded water height above chart datum every six minutes. Table 1 gives the four tide events recorded on one day in March.

Table 1
Event | Clock time | Height (m)
High tide 1 | 03:12 | 2.8
Low tide 1 | 09:26 | 0.6
High tide 2 | 15:40 | 3.1
Low tide 2 | 21:52 | 0.4

Tidal range is the difference in height between a high tide and the low tide that follows it. Table 2 gives the mean tidal range measured at Harbor A during four phases of the Moon, averaged over three years of records.

Table 2
Lunar phase | Mean tidal range (m)
New moon | 3.0
First quarter | 1.8
Full moon | 2.9
Last quarter | 1.7

Table 3 compares four gauging stations along the same stretch of coast. The shape of the basin at each station is described as narrow, meaning the channel tapers inland, or open, meaning it does not.

Table 3
Station | Mean tidal range (m) | Basin shape | Depth at mouth (m)
Harbor A | 2.4 | Narrow | 12
Harbor B | 1.2 | Open | 30
Harbor C | 5.4 | Narrow | 8
Harbor D | 0.5 | Open | 46

When the Sun, Earth, and Moon fall nearly in a line, which happens at new moon and at full moon, the solar and lunar tidal forces add together and produce unusually large spring tides. When the Sun and Moon pull at right angles to each other, at first and last quarter, the two forces partly cancel and produce small neap tides. Local geography matters as well. A narrowing, shallow basin funnels an incoming tide into an ever smaller cross-section, so the water has nowhere to go but up and piles far higher than it would on an open coast of the same latitude.

subject: science
title: Data Representation: Seismic Wave Travel Times
text:
An earthquake releases two kinds of body waves into Earth's interior. P waves, or primary waves, are compressional and travel fastest. S waves, or secondary waves, are shear waves and travel more slowly. Seismographs record the arrival of each. Table 1 gives average travel times to a recording station at several distances from the epicenter, together with the S−P interval, the delay between the two arrivals.

Table 1
Distance (km) | P arrival (s) | S arrival (s) | S−P interval (s)
500 | 78 | 138 | 60
1000 | 138 | 246 | 108
2000 | 246 | 444 | 198
3000 | 341 | 622 | 281
4000 | 427 | 786 | 359

Three stations recorded the same earthquake. Table 2 lists the S−P interval measured at each station and the largest ground motion recorded there.

Table 2
Station | S−P interval (s) | Maximum ground motion (mm)
Denton | 60 | 24.0
Ellis | 198 | 3.6
Fairmont | 281 | 1.5

Table 3 gives the speed of P waves through several materials that make up Earth's interior.

Table 3
Material | P-wave speed (km/s)
Sedimentary rock | 3.5
Granite | 6.0
Basalt | 7.0
Upper mantle | 8.1
Outer core (liquid) | 8.0

Waves that travel farther dive deeper before curving back to the surface, and rock at depth is denser and stiffer, so the average speed along a long path exceeds the average speed along a short one. S waves cannot travel through liquids at all, because a liquid offers no resistance to a shearing motion. As a result no S waves reach the far side of the planet through the liquid outer core, creating a broad S-wave shadow zone. Because the S−P interval lengthens steadily with distance, a single station can estimate how far away an earthquake occurred, but it cannot tell in which direction. At least three stations are needed to fix an epicenter.

subject: science
title: Data Representation: Planetary Albedo and Temperature
text:
Albedo is the fraction of incoming sunlight that a surface reflects rather than absorbs. It runs from 0, meaning all light is absorbed, to 1, meaning all light is reflected. Table 1 lists the albedo, mean surface temperature, distance from the Sun, and atmosphere of five bodies in the solar system. Distance is given in astronomical units (AU), where 1 AU is the mean Earth-Sun distance.

Table 1
Body | Albedo | Mean surface temp (°C) | Distance (AU) | Atmosphere
Mercury | 0.11 | 167 | 0.39 | None
Venus | 0.76 | 464 | 0.72 | Thick CO₂
Earth | 0.31 | 15 | 1.00 | N₂ and O₂
Moon | 0.12 | −20 | 1.00 | None
Mars | 0.25 | −63 | 1.52 | Thin CO₂

Table 2 gives measured albedos for several kinds of surface found on Earth.

Table 2
Surface | Albedo
Fresh snow | 0.85
Sea ice | 0.60
Desert sand | 0.40
Grassland | 0.20
Conifer forest | 0.09
Open ocean | 0.06

A simple energy-balance model was used to estimate Earth's global mean temperature if its planetary albedo were changed while every other factor was held fixed. Table 3 gives the results.

Table 3
Planetary albedo | Modeled global mean temp (°C)
0.25 | 20.4
0.31 | 15.0
0.37 | 9.3
0.43 | 3.1

Albedo and distance together do not fully determine how warm a body is. Venus orbits nearer the Sun than Earth does and reflects roughly three quarters of the sunlight reaching it, yet its surface is the hottest in the solar system, because its dense carbon dioxide atmosphere traps outgoing infrared radiation. The Moon sits at exactly the same distance from the Sun as Earth and has an albedo close to that of Earth's darkest surfaces, yet with no atmosphere at all its mean temperature is 35°C below Earth's.

subject: science
title: Data Representation: Leaf Stomata Density
text:
Stomata are microscopic pores on leaf surfaces through which a plant exchanges carbon dioxide and water vapor with the air. Botanists counted stomata on the lower surface of mature leaves collected from two shrub species, P and Q, growing at five elevations on a single mountainside. Twenty leaves per species per site were examined, and the mean number of stomata per square millimeter was recorded (Table 1).

Table 1
Elevation (m) | Species P (stomata/mm²) | Species Q (stomata/mm²)
100 | 118 | 96
400 | 134 | 108
800 | 152 | 121
1200 | 173 | 139
1600 | 195 | 150

Table 2 lists the mean air pressure and the mean growing-season temperature recorded at each of the five sites.

Table 2
Elevation (m) | Air pressure (kPa) | Mean temperature (°C)
100 | 100.1 | 21.4
400 | 96.6 | 19.5
800 | 92.1 | 17.0
1200 | 87.7 | 14.5
1600 | 83.5 | 12.0

In a separate greenhouse study, Species P was grown from cuttings in four sealed chambers that differed only in carbon dioxide concentration. Every chamber was held at 20°C and 100 kPa and received the same light and water. After 90 days, stomata density and daily water loss per leaf were measured (Table 3).

Table 3
CO₂ (ppm) | Stomata density (stomata/mm²) | Water loss (mg/day)
280 | 186 | 41
400 | 152 | 33
550 | 128 | 26
700 | 109 | 21

Because total air pressure falls as elevation rises, the partial pressure of carbon dioxide available to a leaf falls with it, even though the percentage of CO₂ in air stays nearly constant. Many species compensate by building more pores per unit of leaf area, which raises the rate at which CO₂ can diffuse inward. The greenhouse results show the same relationship running in the opposite direction: when carbon dioxide is abundant, fewer pores suffice, and a leaf with fewer pores also loses less water to the air.

subject: science
title: Research Summaries: Battery Discharge Behavior
text:
Students investigated how rechargeable cells lose voltage as they are discharged. In every trial a fully charged cell was connected to an electronic load that drew a constant current, and terminal voltage was recorded until it fell to a cutoff of 1.0 V. Runtime is the time from the start of discharge until cutoff. Capacity delivered was calculated as current × runtime.

Experiment 1
Three cell chemistries of identical physical size were discharged at 200 mA in a room held at 25°C.

Table 1
Chemistry | Starting voltage (V) | Runtime (h) | Capacity (mAh)
Nickel-cadmium | 1.30 | 4.5 | 900
Nickel-metal hydride | 1.35 | 9.0 | 1800
Alkaline (non-rechargeable) | 1.58 | 10.5 | 2100

Experiment 2
Nickel-metal hydride cells identical to those used in Experiment 1 were discharged at 25°C at four different constant currents.

Table 2
Current (mA) | Runtime (h) | Capacity (mAh)
100 | 18.4 | 1840
200 | 9.0 | 1800
400 | 4.2 | 1680
800 | 1.8 | 1440

Experiment 3
Nickel-metal hydride cells were discharged at 200 mA inside a chamber set to four temperatures.

Table 3
Temperature (°C) | Runtime (h) | Capacity (mAh)
0 | 6.1 | 1220
10 | 7.7 | 1540
25 | 9.0 | 1800
40 | 8.6 | 1720

Voltage did not fall evenly during a discharge. In Experiment 1 the nickel-metal hydride cell held between 1.25 V and 1.20 V for most of its runtime and then dropped sharply in the final minutes, while the alkaline cell's voltage declined steadily from the first hour onward. A device that shuts off below 1.15 V will therefore use almost all of a nickel-metal hydride cell's stored energy but only part of an alkaline cell's. Internal resistance also converts some stored energy to heat, and that loss grows with current, which is why a cell drained quickly delivers less total charge than the same cell drained slowly.

subject: science
title: Research Summaries: Insulation and Heat Loss
text:
A team studied how building insulation slows heat loss. Every test used an identical plywood box of interior volume 0.06 m³ containing a 40 W heater and a thermometer. The box was warmed to 45°C, the heater was switched off, and the interior temperature was recorded while the box sat in a walk-in cold room.

Experiment 1
Boxes were wrapped in fiberglass batting of four thicknesses. The cold room was held at 5°C. Researchers recorded the interior temperature 60 minutes after the heater was switched off and the time required for the interior to fall to 25°C.

Table 1
Insulation thickness (cm) | Temp after 60 min (°C) | Time to reach 25°C (min)
0 | 9 | 14
5 | 21 | 47
10 | 29 | 88
15 | 33 | 121

Experiment 2
Four insulating materials were compared, each applied 10 cm thick, with the cold room again at 5°C.

Table 2
Material | Temp after 60 min (°C) | Time to reach 25°C (min)
Fiberglass | 29 | 88
Cellulose | 27 | 80
Rigid foam board | 34 | 112
Straw bale | 24 | 68

Experiment 3
A box wrapped in 10 cm of fiberglass was tested with the cold room set to three different temperatures.

Table 3
Cold room temp (°C) | Temp after 60 min (°C) | Time to reach 25°C (min)
−5 | 25 | 60
5 | 29 | 88
15 | 34 | 168

The rate at which heat leaves a wall depends on two things: the temperature difference across the wall and the thermal conductivity of the material filling it. A material with lower conductivity moves less heat for the same temperature difference. Still air is an excellent insulator, so materials that trap air in many small pockets, such as fibrous batting and closed-cell foam, outperform solid materials of equal thickness. Pockets large enough to allow circulation lose this advantage, because moving air carries heat across the gap by convection.

subject: science
title: Research Summaries: Yeast Fermentation Rates
text:
Baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) converts sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide when oxygen is scarce. Students measured fermentation rate by sealing a flask with a gas tube that led to an inverted graduated cylinder filled with water, then recording the volume of CO₂ that displaced water from the cylinder.

Experiment 1
Each flask received 5.0 g of dried yeast, 200 mL of water at 30°C, and a different mass of glucose. The volume of CO₂ collected in 30 minutes was recorded, along with the time until the first bubble appeared.

Table 1
Glucose (g) | CO₂ in 30 min (mL) | Time to first bubble (s)
0 | 2 | none observed
2 | 46 | 95
5 | 108 | 61
10 | 187 | 44
20 | 231 | 40
40 | 198 | 52

Experiment 2
Flasks were prepared as in Experiment 1 using 10 g of glucose, then held in water baths set to five temperatures.

Table 2
Temperature (°C) | CO₂ in 30 min (mL)
10 | 31
20 | 96
30 | 187
40 | 205
50 | 44

Experiment 3
Flasks containing 10 g of one sugar and 200 mL of water at 30°C were compared.

Table 3
Sugar | CO₂ in 30 min (mL)
Glucose | 187
Sucrose | 171
Fructose | 179
Lactose | 5

Yeast lacks the enzyme needed to split lactose into usable subunits, so lactose is very nearly unusable as fuel. Above roughly 45°C the proteins that carry out fermentation begin to lose their folded shape, which accounts for the sharp fall recorded at 50°C. Very concentrated sugar solutions create a second problem: they draw water out of yeast cells by osmosis, so the cells shrink and slow down even though fuel is abundant. Bread doughs and wine musts are therefore formulated to keep sugar high enough to feed the yeast but low enough to avoid stalling it.

subject: science
title: Research Summaries: Water Hardness and Cleaning
text:
Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium ions, usually reported as milligrams of calcium carbonate equivalent per liter (mg/L CaCO₃). These ions react with ordinary soap to form an insoluble scum before any lather can develop.

Experiment 1
Five 100 mL water samples of known hardness were placed in stoppered flasks. A standard soap solution was added 0.5 mL at a time, and after each addition the flask was shaken for 10 s. Students recorded the total soap volume needed to produce a lather that lasted 2 minutes, then filtered and weighed the scum.

Table 1
Hardness (mg/L CaCO₃) | Soap needed (mL) | Scum mass (mg)
0 | 0.5 | 0
50 | 2.0 | 18
120 | 4.5 | 44
200 | 7.0 | 76
340 | 11.5 | 128

Experiment 2
Samples drawn from a single 200 mg/L supply were treated in four ways, then tested exactly as in Experiment 1.

Table 2
Treatment | Hardness after (mg/L) | Soap needed (mL)
None | 200 | 7.0
Boiled 15 min, filtered | 140 | 5.0
Passed through ion-exchange resin | 12 | 1.0
Washing soda added | 45 | 2.0

Experiment 3
Experiment 1 was repeated with a synthetic detergent used in place of soap.

Table 3
Hardness (mg/L CaCO₃) | Detergent needed (mL) | Scum mass (mg)
0 | 0.5 | 0
120 | 0.5 | 0
200 | 1.0 | 0
340 | 1.0 | 0

Hardness comes in two forms. Temporary hardness is caused by dissolved bicarbonates, which decompose when the water is heated and settle out as the scale that coats kettles and pipes. Permanent hardness is caused by sulfates and chlorides, which boiling does not remove. Detergent molecules keep their cleaning ability in hard water because their calcium and magnesium salts remain dissolved rather than precipitating.

subject: science
title: Research Summaries: Antibiotic Resistance over Generations
text:
Bacteria can evolve resistance to an antibiotic within a few dozen generations. Resistance is measured as the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), the lowest antibiotic concentration in micrograms per milliliter (µg/mL) that prevents visible growth. A higher MIC means greater resistance.

Experiment 1
A culture of Escherichia coli was grown in broth containing ampicillin at one-half of its current MIC. Every 24 h a sample was transferred to fresh broth containing the same fraction of the new MIC. MIC and colony counts were measured every 10 generations.

Table 1
Generation | MIC (µg/mL) | Colonies per plate
0 | 4 | 210
10 | 9 | 198
20 | 26 | 205
30 | 61 | 190
40 | 88 | 194
50 | 96 | 201

Experiment 2
The procedure of Experiment 1 was repeated with a second culture from the same original stock, grown in broth containing no ampicillin.

Table 2
Generation | MIC (µg/mL) | Colonies per plate
0 | 4 | 214
20 | 5 | 220
40 | 4 | 209

Experiment 3
Cultures taken from generation 50 of Experiment 1 were moved to antibiotic-free broth and grown for 40 further generations. MIC and growth rate, in cell doublings per hour, were then measured. A culture that had never been exposed to ampicillin was grown alongside for comparison.

Table 3
Culture | MIC (µg/mL) | Growth rate (doublings/h)
Never exposed | 4 | 2.05
Generation 50, no recovery period | 96 | 1.42
Generation 50 plus 40 antibiotic-free generations | 71 | 1.78

Resistance genes usually impose a cost. The cellular machinery that pumps an antibiotic back out of the cell, or that rebuilds a damaged target protein, consumes energy that would otherwise support division. When the antibiotic is withdrawn, cells carrying less of this machinery divide faster and gradually outcompete their neighbors, so the average resistance of the population drifts back down, though it rarely returns all the way to the starting value.

subject: science
title: Research Summaries: River Turbidity and Treatment
text:
Turbidity measures how much suspended material clouds a water sample. It is reported in nephelometric turbidity units (NTU), based on how strongly the sample scatters a beam of light. A water utility studied turbidity in the Mill River, which feeds its treatment plant.

Experiment 1
Water samples were collected at a fixed midstream point on days following rainfall of different amounts. River discharge, in cubic meters per second (m³/s), was recorded at the same moment each sample was taken.

Table 1
Rainfall in previous 24 h (mm) | Discharge (m³/s) | Turbidity (NTU)
0 | 4.2 | 6
5 | 6.0 | 18
15 | 11.4 | 74
30 | 22.1 | 210
55 | 38.6 | 465

Experiment 2
A 1.0 L sample of the 465 NTU water was poured into a clear column and left undisturbed. Turbidity was measured at the midpoint of the column at intervals.

Table 2
Settling time (h) | Turbidity (NTU)
0 | 465
1 | 288
3 | 141
6 | 79
12 | 52
24 | 44

Experiment 3
Samples of three different turbidities were passed once through each of three filters at the same flow rate. The table gives the turbidity of the water leaving each filter.

Table 3
Filter | 74 NTU in | 210 NTU in | 465 NTU in
Sand | 9 | 31 | 88
Sand + anthracite | 4 | 12 | 35
Membrane | 0.4 | 0.5 | 0.9

Clay particles only a few micrometers across settle extremely slowly, because drag from the surrounding water nearly balances their weight, so plain settling never clears water completely no matter how long it is given. Treatment plants add coagulant chemicals that neutralize the electric charge holding fine particles apart, allowing them to clump into larger, faster-settling flocs ahead of filtration. The utility's permit requires that water entering the distribution system never exceed 1 NTU.

subject: science
title: Conflicting Viewpoints: What Drives Coral Bleaching
text:
Reef-building corals house single-celled algae called zooxanthellae inside their tissues. The algae supply most of the coral's food through photosynthesis; in return they receive shelter and a steady supply of nutrients. When a coral is stressed it expels the algae and turns white, an event called bleaching. A bleached colony may recover if the stress ends quickly, but prolonged bleaching starves and kills it.

Between 2016 and 2024, divers surveyed Ridge Reef every second year, recording the percent of coral colonies bleached along with two environmental measurements.

Table 1
Year | Colonies bleached (%) | Peak summer sea temp (°C) | Nitrate near reef (µmol/L)
2016 | 41 | 30.8 | 0.9
2018 | 12 | 29.4 | 1.6
2020 | 58 | 31.3 | 1.1
2022 | 9 | 29.1 | 2.4
2024 | 63 | 31.6 | 1.3

Scientist 1
Bleaching at Ridge Reef is driven by heat. Photosynthesis inside the zooxanthellae becomes unstable when water stays more than about 1°C above the long-term summer average of 29.5°C for several weeks. The unstable reactions release reactive oxygen compounds that damage coral tissue, and the coral expels its algae to stop the damage. The survey record fits this mechanism closely. Every year with a peak temperature above 30.5°C bleached more than 40% of colonies, and every year at or below 29.5°C bleached fewer than 15%. Nitrate levels varied from year to year but show no consistent relationship to bleaching at all. Because no local action can lower ocean temperature, reducing greenhouse gas emissions is the only measure that will protect reefs over the long term.

Scientist 2
Heat is a trigger, but it is not the whole story. Corals on remote reefs routinely survive the same temperatures that bleach corals near shore. Nutrient runoff from farms and sewage feeds blooms of fast-growing seaweed that overgrow and shade coral, and it also encourages coral pathogens. Chronic nutrient enrichment lowers the temperature at which a colony bleaches, so an identical warm summer causes far more damage on a polluted reef than on a clean one. The Ridge Reef survey cannot separate the two effects, because nitrate was sampled only once a year and never during the warmest weeks, when the interaction matters most. Cutting local runoff and restoring populations of seaweed-eating fish would raise the bleaching threshold and buy reefs decades of time.

subject: science
title: Conflicting Viewpoints: Decline of the Vernon Aquifer
text:
The Vernon Aquifer supplies drinking water to a growing county. Between 1995 and 2025 the water table beneath the county fell by an average of 14 m. Over the same three decades the county's population tripled, roughly 30% of the aquifer's recharge area was paved or roofed, and average annual precipitation declined. Table 1 summarizes the record by decade.

Table 1
Interval | Water table change (m) | Mean annual precipitation (mm) | Pumping (million m³/yr) | Paved area (%)
1995-2004 | −2 | 870 | 18 | 9
2005-2014 | −5 | 830 | 34 | 19
2015-2025 | −7 | 790 | 46 | 30

Three students propose different explanations.

Student 1
The decline is simply withdrawal outrunning recharge. Pumping rose from 18 to 46 million m³ per year while natural recharge stayed near 30 million m³ per year. Once withdrawal passed recharge, stored water had to fall, and it fell faster as the gap widened. Precipitation and paving did change, but the increase in pumping is by far the largest change in the record, and its timing matches the steepening decline decade by decade. Metering wells and capping total withdrawal at the recharge rate would halt the decline within a few years.

Student 2
The cause is drought. Recharge depends on precipitation, which fell 80 mm between the first and last intervals. Recharge does not fall in proportion to rainfall; it falls much faster, because soil moisture must be satisfied before any water percolates below the root zone. A 10% drop in annual rainfall can cut deep recharge by a third or more. If rainfall returned to its historical average, the water table would stabilize even at current pumping rates, and restricting wells would impose hardship for nothing.

Student 3
Urban surfaces are the key. Rain that lands on pavement and rooftops runs into storm drains and is carried to the river instead of soaking into the ground. Paved area grew from 9% to 30% of the recharge zone, so nearly a third of the land can no longer transmit water to the aquifer regardless of how much rain falls on it. This also explains why the decline steepened most in the final interval, when paving expanded fastest. Requiring permeable pavement and infiltration basins in new development would restore much of the lost recharge without limiting anyone's water use.

subject: science
title: Conflicting Viewpoints: Lichens as Air Quality Indicators
text:
Lichens are partnerships between a fungus and an alga or a cyanobacterium. They absorb water and dissolved gases directly across their surfaces, having no protective waxy cuticle and no roots, so their tissues quickly come to reflect the chemistry of the surrounding air. Ecologists have used lichen surveys as an inexpensive measure of air quality for more than a century, but they disagree about which pollutant matters most today.

A survey of 40 sites in one region recorded the number of lichen species growing on tree trunks, along with air chemistry and bark acidity. Sites were pooled into five groups.

Table 1
Site group | Mean SO₂ (µg/m³) | Nitrogen deposition (kg/ha/yr) | Bark pH | Lichen species
Urban core | 22 | 31 | 4.1 | 3
Inner suburb | 14 | 24 | 4.6 | 7
Outer suburb | 7 | 16 | 5.2 | 14
Rural farmland | 3 | 27 | 5.9 | 11
Remote upland | 1 | 5 | 5.4 | 23

Scientist 1
Sulfur dioxide controls lichen distribution. SO₂ dissolves in the thin film of water on a lichen's surface and forms acid, which destroys chlorophyll in the algal partner and shuts down photosynthesis. Species richness in Table 1 falls as SO₂ rises: 23 species where SO₂ measures 1 µg/m³ and only 3 where it reaches 22 µg/m³. Nitrogen deposition does not track richness nearly as well. Rural farmland receives 27 kg/ha/yr, almost as much nitrogen as the urban core, yet it supports 11 species rather than 3. History agrees with the chemistry: lichens returned to many European cities within a decade after coal smoke controls cut SO₂, long before nitrogen emissions began to fall.

Scientist 2
With SO₂ now low nearly everywhere, nitrogen has become the dominant control, and a simple species count hides what is happening. Nitrogen enrichment does not merely remove lichens; it replaces sensitive species with a handful of nitrogen-loving ones that grow thickly and crowd out the rest. A count cannot detect that substitution unless the species themselves are identified. Nitrogen also alters bark chemistry and changes which fungi can establish in the first place. The rural farmland group makes the point: its SO₂ is nearly as low as the remote upland's, yet it holds only 11 species instead of 23, and its nitrogen load is more than five times higher.
